```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(text2vec)
library(sentimentr)
library(stopwords)
library(knitr)

usc_red  <- "#990000"
usc_gold <- "#E69F00"
blue     <- "#0072B2"

# --- the real corpus: 5,000 IMDB movie reviews that ship with {text2vec} ---
data("movie_review", package = "text2vec")
rv <- as.data.table(movie_review)
rv[, label := ifelse(sentiment == 1, "positive", "negative")]
rv[, clean := gsub("<[^>]+>", " ", tolower(review))]   # lowercase + strip HTML tags
rv[, clean := gsub("\\\\", "", clean)]                  # drop escape backslashes
pos_show <- rv[label == "positive" & nchar(clean) > 150][2]
neg_show <- rv[label == "negative" & nchar(clean) > 150][3]

# --- word counts, before and after stopwords ---
toks  <- word_tokenizer(rv$clean)
vocab <- as.data.table(create_vocabulary(itoken(toks, progressbar = FALSE)))
setorder(vocab, -term_count)
sw <- stopwords::stopwords("en")
vocab[, is_stop := term %in% sw]
top_all    <- vocab[1:15]
top_nostop <- vocab[is_stop == FALSE][1:10]
n_tokens   <- sum(vocab$term_count)
n_terms    <- nrow(vocab)

# --- the 3-review toy corpus for the by-hand slides (made up, tiny on purpose) ---
toy <- data.table(
  doc  = c("A", "B", "C"),
  text = c("great phone great camera",
           "terrible battery terrible screen",
           "great battery"))
toy_long <- toy[, .(word = unlist(strsplit(text, " "))), by = doc]
dtm_toy  <- dcast(toy_long[, .N, by = .(doc, word)], doc ~ word,
                  value.var = "N", fill = 0)
tf_tab <- toy_long[, .N, by = .(doc, word)]
tf_tab[, tf := N / sum(N), by = doc]
df_tab <- toy_long[, .(df = uniqueN(doc)), by = word]
tf_tab <- merge(tf_tab, df_tab, by = "word")
tf_tab[, idf := log(3 / df)]
tf_tab[, tf_idf := round(tf * idf, 3)]

# --- which words separate positive from negative reviews ---
tok_dt <- data.table(doc = rep(seq_len(nrow(rv)), lengths(toks)),
                     word = unlist(toks))
tok_dt[, label := rv$label[doc]]
freq <- tok_dt[!word %in% sw & nchar(word) > 2,
               .N, by = .(label, word)]
freq[, per10k := N / sum(N) * 10000, by = label]
wide <- dcast(freq, word ~ label, value.var = "per10k", fill = 0)
wide <- wide[positive + negative > 8]              # keep reasonably common words
wide[, times_neg := (negative + 0.5) / (positive + 0.5)]
wide[, times_pos := (positive + 0.5) / (negative + 0.5)]
sep_words <- rbind(
  wide[order(-times_neg)][1:6][, .(word, times = -times_neg,
                                   side = "used more in negative reviews")],
  wide[order(-times_pos)][1:6][, .(word, times = times_pos,
                                   side = "used more in positive reviews")])
sep_words <- sep_words[order(times)]
sep_words[, word := factor(word, levels = word)]

# --- sentimentr demo on four sentences ---
demo_sent <- c("This movie is great.",
               "This movie is not great.",
               "Absolutely terrible, I want my money back.",
               "The plot is slow at first, but the ending is fantastic.")
sent_demo <- as.data.table(sentiment_by(demo_sent))
demo_tab <- data.table(Sentence = demo_sent,
                       `Sentiment score` = round(sent_demo$ave_sentiment, 2))

fmt_n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

## Last week's promise {.smaller-90}

Last Tuesday the neural network slide said: in marketing, the fancy models
shine on **text and images**. This week we make good on the text half.

- Reviews, tweets, chat transcripts, survey comments: most of what customers
  tell you arrives as **text**, not as a spreadsheet
- Every model we have used this semester (regression, logit, trees, forests)
  eats **rows and columns of numbers**
- So the whole game today is one move: **turn text into numbers without
  losing what it says**. Once that is done, Thursday's prediction step is
  machinery you already know

## Why marketers care about text {.smaller-90}

- Text reveals **what customers think** (perception), **what happened to
  them** (experience), and **how they feel about it** (emotion), in their
  own words
- What marketing teams do with it: track **brand health** across millions of
  posts, find the **product flaw** behind a wave of one-star reviews, route
  angry support tickets first, detect **fake reviews**
- The scale is the point: no team can read a million reviews, but a model
  can score all of them in minutes

::: {.box}
This is not a new kind of analytics. It is the same pipeline as always,
with one extra step at the front: **text in, numbers out, then the usual
models.**
:::

# From Text to Numbers {.divider}

## The pipeline, start to finish {.smaller-90}

| Step | What it does | Example |
|---|----------|--------|
| **1. Clean** | lowercase, strip punctuation and HTML | "Great movie!" becomes "great movie" |
| **2. Tokenize** | split the text into words | "great movie" becomes ["great", "movie"] |
| **3. Drop stopwords** | remove glue words that carry no meaning | "the", "a", "and" go away |
| **4. Count** | one row per document, one column per word | the bag-of-words matrix |
| **5. Weight** | up-weight distinctive words | TF-IDF |
| **6. Model** | feed the numbers to a model | the logit from week 5, Thursday |

::: {.box}
Steps 1 to 5 are new today. Step 6 is **not new**: once text is a matrix of
numbers, everything from weeks 4 to 9 applies unchanged.
:::

## Our running example: 5,000 movie reviews {.smaller-80}

Real data, loaded live: the `movie_review` dataset that ships with the
`text2vec` R package. `r fmt_n(nrow(rv))` IMDB reviews, each labeled
**positive or negative** (`r fmt_n(rv[label == "positive", .N])` positive,
`r fmt_n(rv[label == "negative", .N])` negative).

Two real examples, shortened:

::: {.smaller-90}
> `r substr(pos_show$clean, 1, 220)`...
> (**positive**)

> `r substr(neg_show$clean, 1, 220)`...
> (**negative**)
:::

::: {.box}
After cleaning, these 5,000 reviews contain about
**`r format(round(n_tokens / 1e6, 1))` million words** drawn from
**`r fmt_n(n_terms)` distinct terms**. Nobody reads that; the pipeline
turns it into a table.
:::

## Steps 1 and 2: clean, then tokenize {.smaller-90}

One sentence, worked through:

| Stage | Result |
|---|---------|
| Raw | `Great movie!! <br /> A must-see... 10/10` |
| Lowercase | `great movie!! <br /> a must-see... 10/10` |
| Strip HTML and punctuation | `great movie a must see 10 10` |
| **Tokenize** (split on spaces) | `great` · `movie` · `a` · `must` · `see` · `10` · `10` |

- Each piece is a **token**. From here on, the model never sees sentences,
  only tokens and their counts
- Real text is dirty: these reviews contain leftover HTML like `<br />`,
  which would otherwise become a nonsense token. **Look at your tokens
  before you model them**

## N-grams: when one word is not enough {.smaller-90}

Splitting into single words destroys word order, and sometimes the order is
the meaning:

- "good" and "**not** good" say opposite things, but as single tokens they
  both contribute the word `good`
- The fix: also count **pairs of consecutive words**, called **bigrams**:
  `not_good` becomes its own token, distinct from `good`
- Single words are **unigrams**; you can go to trigrams and beyond, but the
  number of distinct terms explodes, so most marketing work stops at bigrams

## The most common words {.smaller-90}

```{r freq-before}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_before <- ggplot(top_all, aes(x = term_count, y = reorder(term, term_count))) +
  geom_col(fill = usc_red, width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "The 15 Most Common Words in 5,000 Reviews",
       x = "Times the word appears", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_before
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Every word in all 5,000 reviews, counted. What do you notice about the
words at the top, and how useful would they be for telling a good review
from a bad one?
:::

## Stopwords: the glue gets removed {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r freq-after}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(top_nostop, aes(x = term_count, y = reorder(term, term_count))) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "The Top 10 After Removing Stopwords",
       x = "Times the word appears", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- The raw top 15 was all **the, a, and, of**: grammar glue. These words
  appear in every document, so they cannot separate anything from anything
- Words like these are called **stopwords**, and step 3 simply deletes them
  from a standard list (the list is a choice: in some problems "not" matters,
  so check before deleting it)
- After removal, the top words are **movie, film, story, time**: now the
  counts start to mean something

## Bag-of-words: the counting step {.smaller-80}

Take a tiny, made-up corpus of three phone reviews, and **count every word
in every document**:

- A: "`r toy$text[1]`"
- B: "`r toy$text[2]`"
- C: "`r toy$text[3]`"

```{r dtm-toy}
kable(dtm_toy, align = "lcccccc")
```

- This table is the **bag-of-words matrix**: one row per document, one
  column per word, counts in the cells. Review A **is** the vector
  (0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0)
- "Bag" because order is thrown away: "great phone" and "phone great" give
  the same row. That is the price of turning text into a table

## Bag-of-words at real scale {.smaller-90}

On the real corpus, the same table is `r fmt_n(nrow(rv))` rows by
**`r fmt_n(n_terms)` columns**, one column for every distinct term.

- Almost every cell is **zero**: a 200-word review touches 200 of the
  `r fmt_n(n_terms)` columns. This is called a **sparse matrix**, and R
  stores only the non-zero cells
- Simple and interpretable: every column is a word you can read
- Two problems remain: common words get big counts **just for being
  common**, and `r fmt_n(n_terms)` columns is far more columns than we have
  reviews. The first problem we fix now; the second is **Thursday's whole
  topic**

## TF-IDF: up-weight the words that identify a document {.smaller-80}

A word matters for a document when it is **common in that document but rare
everywhere else**. TF-IDF scores exactly that, in two parts:

- **TF (term frequency)**: how much of document $d$ is word $t$?
  $\text{TF}(t,d) = \frac{\text{count of } t \text{ in } d}{\text{words in } d}$
- **IDF (inverse document frequency)**: how rare is the word across
  documents? $\text{IDF}(t) = \log\frac{N}{\text{docs containing } t}$,
  with $N$ the number of documents. A word in **every** document gets
  $\log(1) = 0$: no weight at all
- **TF-IDF** $= \text{TF} \times \text{IDF}$: big only when both parts are
  big

## TF-IDF by hand, on the toy corpus {.smaller-80}

For document A ("`r toy$text[1]`", 4 words) with $N = 3$ documents:

```{r tfidf-toy}
show <- tf_tab[doc == "A", .(word, `count in A` = N, `TF = count/4` = round(tf, 2),
                             `docs with word` = df,
                             `IDF = log(3/df)` = round(idf, 2),
                             `TF-IDF` = tf_idf)][order(-`TF-IDF`)]
tfidf_great <- show[word == "great"][["TF-IDF"]]
tfidf_phone <- show[word == "phone"][["TF-IDF"]]
kable(show, align = "lccccc")
```

- "great" appears **twice** in A, but it is also in 2 of the 3 documents,
  so its IDF is low: TF-IDF = `r tfidf_great`
- "phone" appears **once**, but **only A** has it: TF-IDF =
  `r tfidf_phone`, the highest score
- That is the whole idea: **"great" is everywhere; "phone" tells you which
  review this is.** The model should listen to "phone" more

## Which words separate good reviews from bad ones {.smaller-90}

```{r sep-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_sep <- ggplot(sep_words, aes(x = times, y = word, fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c(usc_red, blue),
                    c("used more in negative reviews", "used more in positive reviews")),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-8, 4, 2),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "x")) +
  labs(title = "Which Words Tilt Negative, Which Tilt Positive",
       x = "How many times more often the word appears on that side", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
p_sep
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
For every word, we counted how often positive reviews use it and how often
negative reviews use it (per 10,000 words), then took the ratio. "worst" at
8x on the left means negative reviews use it 8 times more often than
positive ones. What do you see?
:::

## Reading the chart {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r sep-chart-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
p_sep + labs(title = NULL)
```

- Negative reviews lean on **worst, waste, awful, stupid**: direct
  complaint words. Positive reviews lean on **excellent, wonderful,
  perfect, amazing**
- Nobody told the data which words are "good": the labels plus simple
  counting surfaced them. This is exactly the signal Thursday's model will
  learn from
- The two sides are not symmetric: the sharpest negative word tilts about
  **8x**, the sharpest positive one only about **4x**. Complaints use
  extreme words; praise words also show up inside negative reviews ("the
  trailer was great, the movie was not"). **No single word decides a
  review**, which is why the model adds up thousands of small signals

## Word embeddings, in plain words {.smaller-90}

Bag-of-words has one blind spot left: to it, "great" and "awesome" are as
unrelated as "great" and "battery": **different columns, nothing shared**.

- **Embeddings** fix that by giving every word a list of, say, 300 numbers
  (a **vector**), learned so that words used in similar contexts get
  **similar vectors**: awesome ends up close to great, far from battery
- They are learned from huge text collections by models like **word2vec**
  (guess the word from its neighbors), and you download them **pretrained**
  rather than training your own
- The trade-off by now is familiar: embeddings capture **meaning** but the
  300 numbers are unreadable; counts are readable but treat every word as an
  island

## Three ways to turn text into numbers {.smaller-80}

| Method | Each document becomes | Strength | Weakness |
|---|-----|------|------|
| **Bag-of-words** | counts over the vocabulary | simple, readable | common words dominate; synonyms unrelated |
| **TF-IDF** | weighted counts | highlights distinctive words; the workhorse | still ignores meaning and order |
| **Embeddings** | an average of word vectors | captures meaning (great is close to awesome) | unreadable numbers; needs a pretrained model |

::: {.box}
Default advice for marketing problems: **start with TF-IDF**. It is fast,
transparent, and with a linear model it is a strong baseline. Reach for
embeddings when synonyms clearly matter and you have the labels to prove
the gain. Thursday we test exactly this on our 5,000 reviews.
:::

# Measuring Opinion: Sentiment {.divider}

## Sentiment: the first thing marketers ask of text {.smaller-90}

- **Sentiment** is the polarity of an opinion: positive, negative, or
  neutral. "Is this review happy or angry?"
- Where it earns money: track **customer satisfaction** without surveys,
  watch a **campaign** land in real time, spot a **brand crisis** while it
  is still small, prioritize the angriest **support tickets**
- Two ways to measure it, and they differ in what they need: a
  **dictionary** or **labeled data**

## Way 1: a dictionary of charged words {.smaller-90}

Lexicon-based sentiment (the `sentimentr` package in R):

- Start from a **dictionary**: thousands of words pre-scored by humans
  (great = +0.75, terrible = -0.75, table = 0)
- Score a sentence by **averaging the scores of its words**
- The good packages also handle **valence shifters**: "**not** great" flips
  the sign, "**absolutely** terrible" amplifies it. This is why they work at
  the sentence level, not word by word

::: {.box}
No training data needed: you can score a million reviews on day one. The
price: the dictionary does not know your domain ("thin" is bad for a
laptop battery and good for a laptop).
:::

## sentimentr, live on four sentences {.smaller-80}

```{r sent-demo}
kable(demo_tab, align = "lc")
```

- Sentence 1 vs. sentence 2: the **"not"** flips a clearly positive score
  to a negative one. A plain word count would have scored both as positive,
  because both contain "great"
- Sentence 3: "absolutely" **amplifies** "terrible", the most negative
  score of the four
- Sentence 4 is the honest case: mixed opinions inside one review average
  out to a mildly positive score. Real reviews are full of this, which is
  why sentence-level scoring beats word counting

## Way 2: train a classifier (Thursday) {.smaller-80}

Supervised sentiment is **week 9 on text features**. Every step is something
you already know:

| Step | What you do | Where you learned it |
|---|---------|-------|
| **1. Label** | each review marked positive or negative (ours already are) | the outcome, week 5 |
| **2. Vectorize** | TF-IDF matrix: 5,000 rows, thousands of word columns | today |
| **3. Split** | train/test, fit on train only | week 9 |
| **4. Classify** | a logit on the word columns | week 5, plus Thursday's fix for "too many columns" |
| **5. Evaluate** | accuracy, precision, recall, AUC on the test set | week 9 |

::: {.box}
When you have labels, the trained model beats the dictionary **in your
domain**: it learns that "thin" is bad for batteries from your own
reviews. Thursday we run this end to end and read which words the model
trusts.
:::

## Beyond positive vs. negative {.smaller-90}

Two directions you should know exist, both one Google away:

- **Emotion detection**: dictionaries that map words to emotions rather
  than polarity (the NRC lexicon tags ~14,000 words with joy, anger, fear,
  trust...). "Which campaign made people excited, and which made them
  anxious?"
- **Topic modeling** (LDA): unsupervised grouping of documents by the words
  they share, clustering for text. "What are the five things people
  complain about?" It finds the themes; **you** name them, exactly like the
  customer segments in week 6

## What text analysis will not tell you {.smaller-90}

- **Sarcasm and context**: "Great, it broke after two days" scores
  positive on words. Dictionaries fall for it; trained models only partly
  escape it
- **The domain shifts**: a dictionary built on movie reviews mis-scores
  banking complaints. Re-check whenever you change domains
- **Volume is not representativeness**: the people who write reviews are
  not your average customers (week 1's Groupon paper all over again)
- **Correlation is not causation**, still: angry reviews predict churn;
  that does not mean the words cause it
